attempts.raw_response: When you do encounter a tricky word, pause and sound it out. If you’re still unsure, make a quick note to check later. Reading aloud in a practice setting can also help—try it with a friend or record yourself. This builds fluency and reduces anxiety. Remember, the goal is understanding, not perfection. Ask questions if something confuses you; that’s how learning deepens. After you finish, summarize the main points in your own words. This reinforces what you’ve absorbed and highlights any gaps. With consistent practice, you’ll find that reading becomes smoother, more enjoyable, and far less intimidating.

pair.human_continuation: Similarly, use a pronunciation guide or look up the pronunciation online if you’re unsure how to say a word. If you have extra time one day, bring your textbook to the nearest reflective surface and read out loud to yourself. You’ll be able to check your own posture, and even practice looking up to make eye contact with yourself. If you have a study buddy, take turns reading important passages to one another. Take breaks to offer constructive feedback. Does your friend not know what to look for? Check in with these questions:  Was your voice clear enough? Is it the right volume? Did it sound timid or confident? Does your body language help you seem more prepared? Are you slouching or standing tall?
pair.prefix: Better yet, read the passage through twice, reading quietly to yourself the second time, if you think you might be called on soon.   Take good notes. You’ll retain information even better once you’ve written it down. Look up unfamiliar words. If you’re reading out loud and get stuck on a big word you didn’t know before, it can break your flow and mess up your confidence.

source_document.title: Be Confident When Reading Out Loud in Class
